It notes in passing that the feature firing on 0.02% of tokens implies at least 1 in 10,000 Pile tokens is a PLoS abbreviation — a fact about the dataset surfaced by a feature.

concepts.name: Attribution similarity
concepts.summary: A third comparison measure that weights a feature's logit effects by whether the feature was actually active and the token actually came next.
concepts.explanation: It is introduced to get at 'the actual effect a feature has on token probabilities' without the cost of full ablations. The paper finds attribution similarity correlates quite highly with activation similarity, meaning features that were coactive across models were useful for predicting the same tokens. That result is what licenses using the cheaper activation correlation as the paper's default universality measure — it stands in for both notions of similarity in this one-layer setting.

concepts.name: Attribution vector
concepts.summary: For each sampled datapoint, the product of a feature's activation there and its logit weight on the token that actually came next.
concepts.explanation: If feature $i$ has logit weights $v_{ik}$ over the vocabulary, then at token $t_j$ the attribution score is $f_i(t_j)\,v_{i t_{j+1}}$, and the attribution vector stacks these scores over a random sample of datapoints. This approximates the classic gradient-times-activation attribution, differing in that it ignores the denominators of the softmax and the layer norm. It is the cheap substitute for computing a full vector of ablation effects for every feature on every datapoint, which the authors say would be computationally expensive.

concepts.name: Matching features to the literature
concepts.summary: A stronger universality test: checking whether features found here resemble units reported in other models by other researchers.
concepts.explanation: The paper finds base64, hexadecimal and all-caps features matching neurons it previously found in one-layer SoLU models, which use a different activation function. It finds a German detector and title case detectors matching features another group found by applying dictionary learning to a residual stream, along with the same preponderance of single-token features. It finds a 'prime factors' feature and a French feature matching results from sparse probing. Matches to multimodal vision-language models are looser — region features for Australia, Canada, Africa and Israel-Palestine loosely mirror reported region neurons, person detectors appear only in very narrow contexts, and no clear analogue of emotion neurons is found.

concepts.name: Multimodal neurons
concepts.summary: Units in vision-language models reported to respond to a concept across images and text, including region, person and emotion neurons.
concepts.explanation: The paper uses these as the most distant comparison point for universality. Region neurons find loose analogues among its features. Person detector neurons — themselves compared to famous single-neuron results in neuroscience — do not: the paper finds features that detect people only in very narrow contexts, such as responding to a name and predicting appropriate next words. No clear analogue of emotion neurons is found. This is one of the places where the paper reports a negative result plainly.

citedFrom.refText: Goh, Gabriel et al. (2021). Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks. Distill
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The specific neuron families being matched against — region, person, emotion neurons — and what evidence established them are defined there.

concepts.name: Sparse probing
concepts.summary: Training sparse linear probes on activations to find whether a property is represented, and by how few neurons.
concepts.explanation: Cited twice: as independent evidence that features may be in superposition, and as a source of features this paper matches — a prime factors feature and a French feature. Sparse probing is a top-down method: you must know what property to probe for. That contrast is part of why the paper values the bottom-up dictionary learning approach, which surfaced distinctions like the three kinds of base64 that nobody would have thought to probe for.

citedFrom.refText: Gurnee, Wes and Nanda, Neel and Pauly, Matthew and Harvey, Katherine and Troitskii, Dmitrii and Bertsimas, Dimitris. Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing. arXiv:2305.01610
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The probing method and the specific features found there are what the universality comparison is being made against.

concepts.name: Finite state automata
concepts.summary: Assemblies of features where one feature raises the probability of tokens that in turn cause another feature to fire on the next step, forming a state machine over generated text.
concepts.explanation: These are not circuits in the conventional sense. The features do not connect through weights inside a forward pass; they connect through the token stream, because a feature's output tokens are the next step's input. The paper adds a second difference: the model did not learn these assemblies to work together. In learning to model text autoregressively it learned features that happen to interact via the token stream because of patterns in the real data. The authors speculate that a model trained with reinforcement learning might have genuine circuits of this shape, whose components co-evolved to work together.

concepts.name: Single-node loop
concepts.summary: The simplest case: a feature that increases the probability of tokens which would themselves activate it again.
concepts.explanation: The base64 feature raises the probability of tokens like 'Qg' and 'zA' — plausible continuations that would keep it firing. That is enough to sustain base64 output once started. The paper stresses these examples come from A/0, the 1× run whose dictionary is not overcomplete; in larger runs the central feature undergoes splitting and the single node becomes a more complex system.

concepts.name: Two-node systems from split Unicode characters
concepts.summary: Where a script's characters are tokenized as a prefix byte plus a suffix byte, the model alternates between a prefix feature and a suffix feature.
concepts.explanation: Tamil characters in block U+0B80–U+0BFF are typically two tokens: 'ண' is '\xe0\xae' followed by '\xa3', where the first part roughly specifies the Unicode block and the second the character within it. So one feature fires on the prefix and predicts suffixes, and another fires on the suffix and predicts prefixes. Chinese is more involved, because many common characters get dedicated tokens while others are split, and the blocks cut across byte boundaries. The key observation the paper offers is that a complete character behaves like a suffix — both can be followed by a new complete character or a new prefix — so one feature covers complete characters and suffixes while the other covers prefixes only. The same two-node shape appears for all-caps snake case, with one feature on the capitalized text tokens and one on underscores.

concepts.name: The four-node HTML system
concepts.summary: Four A/0 features that hand off to each other to generate valid HTML: open tag, tag name, tag close, whitespace, and back to open tag.
concepts.explanation: A/0/20 fires on open tags and predicts tag names; A/0/0 fires on tag names and predicts tag closes; A/0/30 fires on tag closes and predicts whitespace; A/0/494 fires on whitespace and predicts new tag opens. A prototypical sample is something like '<div>\n\t\t<span>'. The paper names the system's obvious shortcoming: it does not describe what happens when A/0/0 emits a token like 'href', which leads to a state the four features do not cover, and looking at A/1 would give something much more complex. A structurally different system exists for IRC transcripts, generating things like '<nickonia_> lol ubuntu ;)', which shows these assemblies are strongly context-specific.

concepts.name: Mechanistic anomaly detection
concepts.summary: The idea of noticing when a model's internal mechanism behaves differently in a specific narrow case.
concepts.explanation: Raised in connection with the phrase-memorizing features: a feature that is near-binary and fires only on one specific legal phrase is exactly a mechanism that activates in a narrow case, which is what such detection would look for. The paper offers this as a framing rather than an implementation — it does not build a detector.

citedFrom.refText: Christiano, Paul (2022). Mechanistic anomaly detection and ELK.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The proposal and what it would require are defined there; the paper only names it as an analogy.

concepts.name: Theories of superposition, revised
concepts.summary: The paper's reassessment of the picture it inherited: features clump into dense related groups and may not be one-dimensional, which the earlier toy picture did not anticipate.
concepts.explanation: Discussion opens by naming the inherited view — the isotropic model — and saying this work persuaded the authors it was missing something. At minimum, features clump into higher-density groups of related features. Two explanations are offered, correlated activations and shared downstream actions, with the second suspected to be more central. Beyond clumping, the authors question whether features are one-dimensional at all, raising higher-dimensional feature manifolds. They note the hypotheses are not mutually exclusive: the convex hull of several correlated features could be read as a manifold, though some manifolds would not admit any finite description in terms of one-dimensional features.

concepts.name: Isotropic superposition model
concepts.summary: The inherited picture from Toy Models: features are discrete, one-dimensional, and repel each other through interference into a roughly evenly spaced arrangement of directions.
concepts.explanation: Each of its three commitments is questioned by this work. Discrete and one-dimensional is challenged by feature manifolds and by feature splitting that never seems to stop. Evenly spaced is challenged directly by the observed clusters of features with small angles between directions. The paper does not discard the model — it says the experiments left it more confident that some version of superposition is true — but concludes the toy models work is missing an important dimension of the problem by not studying highly correlated, action-sharing features.

concepts.name: Action-sharing features
concepts.summary: Features that produce similar downstream effects and therefore end up with similar directions — the paper's suspected main cause of feature clustering.
concepts.explanation: The worked case: the feature firing on single digits in base64 predicts approximately the same set of tokens as the feature firing on other base64 characters, except for other digits. Similar downstream effects manifest as geometrically close feature directions, because producing similar output actions requires producing similar neuron activations. Combined with the features also being highly correlated in when they fire, this gives real models both denser and more structured superposition than the toy models predicted. Toy Models did study correlated features, but only correlation in whether they are active, with no analogue of shared output actions.

concepts.name: Correlated features
concepts.summary: Features that tend to fire together, offered as one explanation for why feature directions clump.
concepts.explanation: This is the explanation the authors consider less central than shared actions, though they note the two are not exclusive. Toy Models had examined correlated features, including how correlation organizes feature directions and how strongly correlated features can collapse into a single broader feature. The paper flags that collapsing-versus-tight-superposition distinction as the useful intuition to carry over: two similar features held separately in tight superposition is a different situation from one broader feature.

concepts.name: Feature manifolds
concepts.summary: The possibility that some features are not one-dimensional intensity scales but higher-dimensional continuous families of related directions.
concepts.explanation: The inherited picture has each feature encoding only an intensity along a fixed direction. The paper raises the alternative that a set of related features forms a continuous surface in activation space. The convex hull of several correlated features could be understood this way, but the authors note the reverse does not hold: some manifolds would not admit a unique description in terms of any finite number of one-dimensional features. They suggest this might account for the continued feature splitting they observe — if the underlying object is continuous, no finite dictionary ever finishes resolving it.

concepts.name: Is there a correct number of features?
concepts.summary: Under some expanded theories the question is not well posed; under others there is a true number but getting it exactly right is not essential.
concepts.explanation: The paper separates two cases. If features form continuous manifolds, asking for the correct count may have no answer. If there is a true finite set, the consequence of getting the count wrong is mild — the process 'fails gracefully', showing the true features at different granularities as the dictionary grows. Either way the practical upshot is the same: dictionary size is a resolution knob rather than a parameter that must be tuned correctly.

concepts.name: Local versus compositional codes
concepts.summary: Two ways to represent a combination of properties: one unit per combination (local), or separate units that combine (compositional).
concepts.explanation: Representing 'the in Physics' with its own feature is technically a local code. The more intuitive scheme would be a compositional code, with 'the' as one feature and 'Physics' as another, and the combination read off from both firing. Local codes are sparser than compositional ones — a single unit carries the whole conjunction — which matters because the autoencoder is trained with a sparsity penalty. The paper borrows this vocabulary explicitly to make its question about token-in-context features precise.

citedFrom.refText: Olah, Christopher (2023). Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The local/compositional vocabulary and examples are taken from there and used without full definition.

concepts.name: Local code
concepts.summary: A representation with one dedicated unit per thing represented, including per combination of properties.
concepts.explanation: Sparse by construction — one unit active per represented item — which makes it the code an L1 penalty tends to favor. The paper's token-in-context features are local codes over token-context pairs. Its argument that this may be genuine rests on prediction sharpness: a dedicated unit for a pair can output whatever distribution it likes for that pair.

concepts.name: Compositional code
concepts.summary: A representation where independent units combine to represent a conjunction — 'the' and 'Physics' active together.
concepts.explanation: More economical in units, and the arrangement one would intuitively expect. Its constraint is that downstream effects add: if token and context are independent features, the resulting logits must be the sum of their separate contributions. That additivity is exactly what the paper argues the model may not want.

concepts.name: Are token-in-context features real?
concepts.summary: Whether the hundreds of 'the'-in-a-context features reflect the transformer's own local code, or an artifact of dictionary learning imposing one.
concepts.explanation: The paper states two hypotheses cleanly. Either the transformer uses a compositional code and a quirk of the dictionary learning scheme renders it as a local one — in which case a better scheme could recover the compositional features, and the L1 penalty may be pushing too far toward sparsity. Or the transformer genuinely uses a local code at least in part, and dictionary learning is representing it correctly. The authors say they believe the second holds to some extent, while conceding the first is a live possibility. This is one of the paper's more explicit uncertainties about its own method.

concepts.name: The sharper-predictions argument
concepts.summary: The reason to think local codes are real: a compositional code forces the logits for 'the in Physics' to be a sum of two generic contributions, while a dedicated feature can be more specific.
concepts.explanation: If 'the' and Physics context were represented independently, the model's output would have to be 'upweight tokens which come after the' plus 'upweight tokens which occur in Physics'. A dedicated 'the in Physics' feature can instead predict exactly the noun phrases that follow 'the' in physics writing. The paper argues the model might want predictions sharper than the sum allows, and that only a local code makes that possible. The feature splitting results support this: split features have visibly more specific top logits than their parents.

concepts.name: Scalability of analysis
concepts.summary: The barrier that would remain even if sparse autoencoders fully solved superposition: turning microscopic feature-level insight into a macroscopic understanding of a model.
concepts.explanation: The authors ask directly whether solving superposition would be a home run and answer no — at least one other fundamental barrier remains. Automated interpretability is one candidate route, though they say delegating the understanding of AI to AI may not be fully satisfying for various reasons. The alternative they gesture at is discovering larger-scale structure among features, so that analysis can operate on groups rather than individual features.
